title: The Nashik cave inscription of Ushavadata
body: The Nashik cave inscription (2nd century CE) of Ushavadata, son-in-law of the Shaka king Nahapana, records that he gave a cave to the Buddhist Samgha and also a perpetual endowment of 3,000 kahapanas. The money was meant to provide cloth money and other needs for monks of any sect or origin living in the cave. The donor did not hand the coins to the monks directly. Instead, 2,000 kahapanas were invested in a weavers' guild at Govadhana at an interest of one pratika per hundred every month, and 1,000 kahapanas were invested in another weavers' guild at an interest of three-quarters of a padika per hundred every month. The interest, not the deposit itself, was to be used year after year to maintain the monks and the caves.
